newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals drives wedge into Japan cobalt market.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals drives wedge into Japan cobalt market.

text.p: U.S. trader Minor Metals Inc has driven a wedge into Japan's huge cobalt market, while its European arch-rival Glencore International AG awaits the start of production at its Australian mine, Japanese traders say.

"Minor Metals has boosted its share in Japan," said a trader at one of Japan's major trading houses. "It's difficult for others, such as Glencore, to move in unless they can match offers by Minor Metals."
Traders say Minor Metals has aggressively expanded its business in Japan, at times offering cobalt at about 10 percent below prevailing market prices.
Officials at Minor Metals and Glencore Far East AG here were not available for comment on cobalt, which in Japan is used mainly in lithium-ion batteries and video tapes.

Traders say that in order to guarantee smooth and flexible deliveries, a key for satisfying fastidious Japanese clients, Minor Metals has built up substantial stocks in Japan, the world's second-largest cobalt consumer after the United States.
The trade house also offers an unusual system of consignment, allowing clients to reserve a portion of its stocks while paying only for the amount they actually use, the traders added.

Glencore, which clashed head-on with Minor Metals in the world cobalt market last year, will not be ready for serious battle until the Murrin Murrin nickel project in Australia starts turning out an expected 3,000 tonnes of cobalt per year in 1999, traders said.
They added that it is extremely difficult to gain a foothold in the Japanese market, still dominated by a few domestic trading houses acting as agents for the top world producers.
"At the moment, Glencore is not a major player. It is only bringing to Japan African and Russian product it acquired in Europe," one trader said.
"But once production starts (at Murrin Murrin), Glencore can emerge as strong as any other agent," he added.

In November, Glencore acquired 40 percent of the Murrin Murrin nickel-cobalt project, which the project's developer, Anaconda Nickel NL, says can expand its annual cobalt output to more than 4,500 tonnes by the year 2000.

Market sources said Minor Metals chief Rami Weissfisch was in Japan in May, when cobalt prices were flying high due to a civil war in the former Zaire and a suspension of U.S. stockpile sales following legal complaints by Minor Metals.
"He not only visits Japanese users, but approaches Japanese trading houses, as it's difficult for a foreign company to develop ties with small users," an industry source said.
"Some trade houses, agents for African suppliers, have secretly introduced their clients to Minor Metals as their clients were hit by lower African production," he added.

Minor Metals' expansion came at a time when Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, formerly Zaire, struggled with falling production due to a lack of investment, declining ore grades, strikes and civil unrest.

Official data show that cobalt production in the Congo, which spent more than three decades under the dictatorial rule of former president Mobuto Sese Seko, slumped to a mere 4,000 tonnes last year from a peak of 14,518 tonnes in 1986.

Accordingly, Japanese cobalt imports from the two African countries in 1996, at 2,600 tonnes, were little changed from 2,300 tonnes in 1992, while Japan's consumption surged to 5,700 tonnes from 3,600 during the same period, according to Mitsui & Co Ltd.
"As production in (former) Zaire and Zambia plunged, the Japanese market lost a few key players. There's room for traders to expand their business now," said a trader at another major trading house.

Traders say other trade houses besides Minor Metals and Glencore are also eyeing Japan, which as the world's top battery maker is set to overtake the United States in the near future as the metal's largest consumer.
"We are convinced that 10,000 tonnes per year of cobalt consumption in Japan is possible at the beginning of the 21st century," Mitsui said in a recent report.
